title: Guide to field note-taking

You will have to keep track of a lot of information. You are less likely to lose track of that information if you set up your notebook so that you won’t forget.






Prep for each field day!

Before heading out, you can list the important metadata to have, format your pages, etc. so that by the time you are in the field, all you have to do is fill in the information.

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Notebook organization


edited 2026-10-19: added some information on organization
On Mondays, you will be responsible for participating in site presentations. This includes taking notes in your notebook.
On Tuesdays in the field, you will be recording your observations in your notebook. Your field notebook is the repository for all the information you will be learning in the field. It is very important to keep it organized!
Each field day should include:

Metadata
Species account
Observations and field notes
Post-field day reflection

Your species account and observations with field notes will be completed in class. Your post-field day reflection will be done outside of class.






Leave yourself space to reorganize!



It is normal for your field notes to be a little messy as you’re taking them. If you need to rewrite any notes in your species accounts or observations, then build in the space in your layout to do so.

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Metadata
“Metadata” is information about information. Metadata provides broad context for the information you record in your notebook. For each field day, you should record:

Date
Time (start and end)
Location
Number of people in group
Weather (qualitative description)

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Species accounts
In the field, we will walk around and identify organisms of varying taxonomic groups to get a sense of how a habitat or ecosystem is structured.
Your species account should be organized in a table; you can draw this in your notebook prior to the field day so that you can keep track of the species we discuss.
Each species account section should be organized with the following information in organized columns:

species
number of individuals
identifying characteristics
behavior, phenology, location, etc.
notes







Priorities in the field



You may find that your notes get messy when you’re taking down information in the field. That is ok! If your species accounts get messy, take time after class to copy your notes onto clean pages in your notebook.
You will receive feedback to incorporate this practice into your maintenance of your field notebook during the notebook checks if your species accounts are particularly messy.

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Observations and field notes
Field notes and observations are the core of this class. Good notes document species observations (what did you see), behaviors/trends/phenomena (what was it doing), and the context for those observations (where did you see what you saw, at what time of day/year). Field notes also signify what you think is important to document; you are assigning value to information when you’re deciding whether or not to write it down.
Above all, field notes must be honest and accurate. This means that you have documented what you have sincerely tried to understand as true, incorporating information from your own perspective, others’ perspectives, and other sources of information (e.g. field guides, literature).

title: Guide to field note-taking
text:
Post-field trip reflection
Each field trip should be accompanied by a reflection, which takes the form of a diary format chronicling the trip using information from the notes you take in the field (this is why it’s important to keep good field notes!).
Each reflection should start with the date and time you complete the reflection (I recommend the same-day or day after, when things are fresh in your memory).
The content of the reflection should include:

A narrative account of the trip: where we went at the site, where we stopped to conduct detailed observations, etc.
New experiences for you: for example, a new organism, drawing, conversation with someone in the class, identification, etc.
How you improved in a skill: for example, drawing a diagram, composing an observation page, keeping track of all your personal items, etc.

All reflections should be done in your field notebook.

text:

You will be responsible for briefing your peers on one site. Sign up for a site presentation here.
Aim for 25-30 minutes for your site presentation. This includes the time you allocate for discussion and questions - plan accordingly!

title: Site presentations
text:
Your responsibilities
Prior to giving your site presentation, you should:

complete any readings on Canvas
read the chapter relating to your site’s ecosystem and/or management from Ecosystems of California
coordinate with your site presentation partner on:

how you would like to work together on your presentation
when you would like to meet with An to check in about your presentation

explore observations from your site on iNaturalist







Ecosystems of California



Much of the ecological information you will need to digest and relay to your peers is in Ecosystems of California (edited by Harold Mooney and Erika Zavaleta). The book can be accessed online via the UCSB Library for free. To access the book, you must be connected to the campus wireless network, logged in via the library proxy, or connected to a campus VPN. See An if you need help with any of these options.

title: Site presentations
text:
What to include
All site presentations should be in the form of Google or Powerpoint slides (except for the presentation done in the field). Your presentation should include (not necessarily in this order):

Basic information

the site name
the dominant ecosystem type (this can be tricky to categorize, so you may consider listing a few different types but focusing on one)
the features (e.g. geological, plant community) that define that/those ecosystem type(s)
services provided by this ecosystem type (e.g. carbon sequestration, flooding mitigation) with an explanation of why that occurs
management information (i.e. who manages the site)
threats to this ecosystem type, and potential solutions



Background

the geological features/history of the ecosystem type (enough to understand why certain plants may occur there or distinguishing features are present)
the ecological background of the ecosystem type, including

2-3 examples of other sites of the same ecosystem type
a discussion of how these sites differ or are similar to the field site
potential interactions between species communities within this ecosystem type (e.g. predation, herbivory, competition)

the history of human disturbance and interaction with this ecosystem type



Species occurrences

commonly recorded plant species on iNaturalist that are distinguish this site/habitat
potential sightings of birds, mammals, herps, arthropods (not all of these - choose a taxonomic group that you and your partner are interested in)



Additional components

1-2 group discussion questions based on the class readings and your chapter of Ecosystems of California
at least 1 figure from the readings or text presenting data that is relevant to the topic you want to highlight (see An if you need help identifying a figure)







Prepping discussion questions



Prior to your presentation, make a one-on-one appointment (or come to drop-in hours) with An to check in about your discussion questions. This is strongly recommended (but not required) to make sure that you’re on track.




Presentation style
Independently of the material you present, you should be considering:

presentation of text: are there too many words on the slides? Too few?
presentation of visuals: are you using pictures, maps, etc. effectively? Are the visuals tied clearly to the points you are making?
cohesion: are all the fonts, sizes, faces (e.g. normal, italics, bold) consistent? Is the formatting consistent across slides?
oral presentation: are you and your partner speaking for approximately equal amounts of time? Are you stopping for questions from the audience?
aesthetics: have you designed your slides in an aesthetically pleasing way? Have you expanded your presentation past the default settings on your platform of choice?
integration and transitions: are all the pieces of your presentation arranged in a way that is easy to follow? does each topic flow smoothly to the next?

title: Interpretive sign - final draft
text: Due Monday 30 November at the beginning of class

title: Interpretive sign - final draft
text:
Overview and goals

What is an interpretive sign?
Interpretive signs are often placed along trails to educate people passing by about what they are observing, and often communicate why it is important to study or protect an area or species. For example, Campus Lagoon has many interpretive signs explaining the diﬀerent habitats in the area and species that CCBER works to restore. These signs serve to provide information to the public about what work is currently happening at the lagoon and why it is important. For example, visitors reading a sign about bioswales will know why CCBER employees are working to construct these wetlands around Manzanita Village.


Goals
Your final interpretive sign should communicate two main messages to the audience (visitors to the field site): 1) why these species are worth conserving/studying and, and 2) why this habitat is worth conserving/studying.
To communicate these messages to the audience, you should include, at minimum:

a wide view of the ecosystem: what is the landscape or dominant ecosystem types?
plant species that occur at that ecosystem: what plants are common in this ecosystem type? How do they characterize the ecosystem?
faunal species that occur at that ecosystem at different trophic levels: what species occur at the site, and how do they interact (with each other and with the environment)?

You will also demonstrate your ability to distill sources of information for a broad audience. At this point in the quarter, you have experience reading many different kinds of texts: original studies, reviews, field guides, etc. In this assignment, you will integrate information from a variety of sources to tell a story about an ecosystem.

title: Interpretive sign - final draft
text:
Examples
See these examples of interpretive trail signs here. Note: student examples are from an assignment with slightly different parameters, but demonstrate the communication mode and core message of the interpretive sign you will create.

title: Interpretive sign - final draft
text:
Basic components

Sign
Your sign must be hand made and written. Take this into account when you are designing the layout.
The final dimensions should be _______________.
Your sign should include:

a title
sections with text (500-600 words across all sections) explaining:

species or interaction(s) of interest, and why they are important to understand
why the field site and/or habitat of interest is important to conserve/protect
how humans historically interacted with the site or ecosystem
how humans currently interact with the site or ecosystem

your own visuals, including at minimum (but not limited to):

a depiction of the field site in a map, landscape, or cross-section
the species of interest




Cited text
Most interpretive trail signs do not have citations. Yours shouldn’t either! As part of your final submission, you will create a separate document recreating the text on your sign with added citations.
This component may be typed.
Your cited text should include:

the same text you present on your sign
in-text citations
a Works Cited or Reference page with

consistently formatted citations using one of the following options: 1) American Psychological Association (APA), 2) Modern Language Association (MLA), or 3) Chicago Manual of Style format


Prior to citing your sources, you should verify that they are published articles, books, etc. For this assignment, you must correctly cite at least:

one original study (i.e. a work in which data are presented), and
one book (e.g. a field guide, textbook, manual)

title: Interpretive sign - final draft
text:
Presentation
The presentation of information in your interpretive sign will be evaluated on:

cohesion: all text and visuals have a cohesive look
narrative: your writing depicts the species, site, and ecosystem accurately with evidence to support your claims, appropriate for the audience (visitors to the field site)
written communication: your writing is clear, free of grammatical errors

title: Interpretive sign - final draft
text:
Creativity
As with your field guide, you can and should be creative in the way you present information for your interpretive sign. This component is reflective of your process in creating an interpretive sign for your field site of interest. Creativity will be evaluated on the novelty with which you have presented your work and the execution of your original vision. You will make a case for both these points in your self-evaluation.

title: Interpretive sign - planning
text: Due Tuesday 10 November at the beginning of class

title: Interpretive sign - planning
text:
Overview
Your second class project is an interpretive trail sign. This can be an expansion on your field guide, or you can use this opportunity to learn about a new ecosystem or site.
You do not have to make your sign for a class field site. The only requirement is that your site is situated in California.
Prior to completing this planning assignment, read the final directions for the interpretive sign and review the examples linked in the directions.

title: Interpretive sign - planning
text:
Assignment

Basic information
In 1-3 sentences each, outline your ideas for the following:

the site on which you want to focus
the dominant ecosystem at that site
why you are interested in this site or ecosystem
historical human interaction with the site or ecosystem
current human interaction with the site or ecosystem



Species of interest
For each of these components, describe why they are relevant to the site and ecosystem. Note that you may write more than 3 sentences for these components if needed.

2-3 primary producers
2-3 consumers
2-3 predators



Visual representations
Note that you may write more than 3 sentences for these components if needed.
Describe how you plan to visually represent:

the “wide view” of the ecosystem (examples include but are not limited to: map, landscape, cross-section), and why
species of interest and their interactions with each other and the environment



Outline
Lastly, draw a potential layout for your interpretive sign. Use stick figures or coarse sketches for visual components, and shapes representing placeholders for each written section (including the title).

title: Independent field trip option 2: estuaries
text: Due Tuesday 17 November at the beginning of class

title: Independent field trip option 2: estuaries
text:
Overview
Carpinteria Salt Marsh is the field site for week 7. Carp Salt Marsh and Devereux Slough (at NCOS/COPR) are examples of estuaries - specifically salt marshes - which are key coastal ecosystems. In this independent field trip option, you will visit another estuary close to campus: Goleta Slough. Choose this option if you are interested in ecosystems bridging marine and freshwater aquatic systems.
You will turn in a hard copy of this assignment in class. If you don’t want to turn in your entire notebook, do this assignment separately from your notebook.

title: Independent field trip option 2: estuaries
text:
Locations
You will walk, bike, or otherwise travel to three points relating to Goleta Slough, all within 1 mile of Henley Gate: 1) Tecolotito Creek Bridge, 2) pond at Atascadero Creek bend, and 3) the mouth of the slough.

title: Independent field trip option 2: estuaries
text:
Assignment overview






Don’t forget your metadata!







a. Create a species account.
At each of these points, identify as many species as possible in one taxonomic group to characterize the habitat in which you find yourself.
Take at least 15 minutes for your species accounts.


b. Conduct an observation.
Choose two points at which you want to closely observe an organism, species, or interaction.
Take at least for minutes on your observation.


c. Write your post-field day reflection.
In your reflection, compare what you saw at Goleta Slough with Carpinteria Salt Marsh and Devereux Slough. Discuss how they compare in:

water source
water level
species richness (i.e. number of species)
community composition (i.e. species present)

Discuss why you may have observed any similarities or differences (e.g. shared habitats, common plants, time of day of visit).

title: Independent field trip option 2: estuaries
text:
Checklist
By the due date, you should have:

metadata for your field day
species accounts for all three points on the map
an observation from two points of your choosing
a post-field day reflection

You will turn in a hard copy of your species accounts, observations, and reflections in class on Tuesday the 17th of November.

title: Field guide - self evaluation
text: Due Monday 2 November at the beginning of class

title: Field guide - self evaluation
text:
Overview
This is the self-evaluation that accompanies your final field guide. This should be a separate document (i.e. not included within the pages of your field guide).
The self-evaluation is a venue for you to explain in your own words your choices in creating your field guide and how they reflect your independent thinking.

title: Field guide - self evaluation
text:
Assignment
Explain each point in 2-5 sentences each.

Visuals

How do the visuals and chosen characteristics to highlight demonstrate your understanding of field identification for the species you chose?
How does the visual representation (e.g. color, arrows, written annotation) draw attention to the characteristics you listed above?



Sources of information

How do your cited sources support the information you present in your field guide? Provide at least one specific example of a claim you made and the source supporting that claim.
How did your own field observations - in class or otherwise - contribute to the representation of species in your field guide? Provide at least one specific example of an observation you made and how it translated to a choice you made in your field guide.



Creative process

How do your creative choices represent what you are drawn to in books, visual art, etc.? Provide at least one specific example of a source of inspiration for the creative components of the field guide and how that source influenced your work.
How did you translate written information into your own voice? In other words, how do you think the narrative components of this assignment reflect your perspective in writing? Provide at least one example of how the writing you present in your field guide mirrors the writing you have done in other venues (e.g. your field notebook).



Feedback

What kinds of feedback did you receive on your first draft? How did you incorporate that feedback? If you didn’t, why not?







Considering feedback



Feedback can be useful for improving your work! The comments you receive from your peers and from me (An) are meant to help make your work better. However, you may disagree with some comments - this is normal. For any points you disagree with, you should be able to articulate why you didn’t think incorporating that feedback would improve your work, in your perspective.

title: Detailed outline
text: Hard copy due at the beginning of class on Tuesday 13 October

title: Detailed outline
text:
Overview
This is the third of four project prep assignments for the field guide assignment. Previously, you drew multiple interaction diagrams and hypothesized about the potential interactions between species in your focal taxonomic group. In this assignment, you will create a detailed outline of the layout and the text for your field guide.
To have some flexibility in layout, this assignment may be done digitally or by hand. If you choose to complete your assignment digitally, make sure to factor in the time to print it out. Note that your final field guide must be hand made and written.






Free printing resources on campus



Use GauchoPrint to print for free!

title: Detailed outline
text:
Before starting this assignment

Read the final field guide requirements.
Make sure you understand the components you will need to incorporate for your field guide.






Choose your site × taxonomic group!



In the last assignment, you explored potential relationships between species in your chosen taxonomic group at your site. Before proceeding, choose one with which to move forward.

title: Detailed outline
text:
Assignment

1. Create a mock up of the layout.
In your choice of medium (e.g. Canva, Google Slides, Word doc, pen and paper), create a mock layout of all the pages in your field guide. Use boxes or other shapes to denote areas of the page in which you intend to place an image or text. Label any shapes with what will occupy that space.
Keep in mind that:

you are not locked into the layout you create here; this is meant for you to be able to visualize your field guide prior to starting the final draft.
you do not need to create full page layouts for each page of your field guide; feel free to use half size pages.



2. Outline the text.






Differences between an outline and a draft



Outlined text is in bullet points representing ideas that you will eventually express in full sentences in a draft. The outline you create here will be the foundation off of which you build your first draft (due next week).
In this assignment, you are expected to have text in bullet point form.


Outline the text for each species entry. For each of the species you have chosen for your field guide, you should have bullet points outlining the:

species description
habitat description
ecological description
some citations (these don’t have to be full citations; you’re just providing basic information on the sources from which you are pulling this information)







How many bullet points do I need for each section?



Unfortunately, this depends. You should have enough information in your outline to receive feedback; thus, your bulleted ideas should be clear enough such that someone (An) can read your outline to give you comments, but be unstructured and flexible enough to change.








Finding sources of information



You can use published books or peer-reviewed articles as sources. Existing field guides are great places to start!
You can also look at citations from species pages. iNaturalist pages have lots of cited peer-reviewed papers. For example, this iNaturalist page for the North American Mountain Lion has all the sources listed at the bottom. While not all sources may be relevant to you, you can use these as starting points to find your own information.




3. Describe how you plan to incorporate visuals.
Each species entry should have a visual representation of the species. In 1-3 sentences, describe how you plan to create your visuals (e.g. photograph organisms yourself, draw, paint).

title: Detailed outline
text:
Checklist
By the due date, you should have:

a layout of all the pages in your field guide from part 1
an outline of your species entries from part 2
written response to part 3

As a reminder: this assignment may be done digitally or by hand. You will turn in the paper copy of your work in class on Tuesday.

title: Interaction diagram
text: Due Tuesday 6 October at the beginning of class

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Overview
This is the second of four project prep assignments for the field guide assignment. Previously, you selected two site × taxonomic group combinations and described why you were interested in those sites/groups. In this assignment, you will explore the potential relationships between species you selected and other species that may occur at that site. You will depict relationships between species using an interaction diagram that will ultimately appear in your final field guide.


edited 2026-09-30: there are four project prep assignments, not five as previously stated.
All components of this assignment should be done by hand on paper.

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Before starting this assignment

Read “Direct and Indirect Interactions” by Moon, Daniel C. et al. from Nature Education Knowledge.
Read the species descriptions for your species in the appropriate field guide or textbook. This may include (but is not limited to):

plants: The Jepson Manual edited by BG Baldwin, California Plants by Matt Ritter, A Californian’s guide to the trees among us by Matt Ritter
birds: Field guide to Birds of Western North America by Sibley
reptiles: Field Guide to Amphibians and Reptiles of California by Stebbins and McGinnis
mammals: Mammals of North America by Kays and Wilson
invertebrates: Field Guide to California Insects by Will, Gross, Rubinoff, and Powell








Use library resources!



All the books listed above are available in hard copy or online via the library.

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Assignment

1. Draw and describe one ecological relationship for each of your taxonomic groups.
Choose one pair of species from each taxonomic group. Consider the flow of energy between both species. For each pair, draw the appropriate arrows connecting the two species in the pair.
For each pair, explain in 2-3 sentences why you drew the interaction in that way, using information about the morphology, phenology, habitat, and/or behavior of each species. Be specific about the characteristics you used to categorize the interaction. Provide citations for information about species characteristics and any other details you found from the literature.


2. Draw interaction diagrams between all the species you chose for each taxonomic group.
You should have two interaction diagrams - one for each group - with arrows connecting each species. With new species, the flow of energy may change from the diagram you drew in part 1 (though it may stay the same!).
For each diagram, explain in 2-3 sentences why you think those interactions exist, using characteristics of each species to justify your thinking. As above, be specific about the characteristics you used to categorize the interaction and provide citations.


3. Draw interaction diagrams incorporating three new species not included in your core species list.
Recreate each diagram you drew in part 2 with two additional species outside of your focal taxonomic group.
For each diagram, explain in 3-5 sentences - how and why you chose the new species - how the diagram has changed with the addition of the new species
Be specific about the characteristics of the species that inform your choice of interaction. Provide citations as needed.

title: Interaction diagram
text:
Checklist
By the due date, you should have:

drawings and written responses for part 1
drawings and written responses for part 2
drawings and written responses for part 3

As a reminder: all components of this assignment should be done by hand in pen, pencil, or other writing implement on paper. You will turn in the paper copy of your work in class on Tuesday.

title: Independent field trip option 1: (sub)urban parks
text:
Overview
Lake Los Carneros (LLC) in Goleta is the field site for week 4. LLC is one example of a built green space that provides wildlife habitat and space for human recreation. In this independent field trip option, you will visit and conduct a field observation at four parks in Isla Vista. Choose this option if you are interested in urban planning and the incorporation of green spaces in residential areas.
You will turn in a hard copy of this assignment in class. If you don’t want to turn in your entire notebook, do this assignment separately from your notebook.

title: Independent field trip option 1: (sub)urban parks
text:
Assignment overview






Don’t forget your metadata!







a. Create a species account.
Walk around the park and identify as many species as possible to characterize the park’s habitat. Note that this will differ based on the park!


b. Conduct an observation.
At one park, choose an organism, species, or interaction to focus on observing.
Spend at least 20 minutes on your observation.


c. Write your post-field day reflection.
In your reflection, compare the four parks you visited with LLC. Discuss how they compare in:

size
diversity of habitat types

Discuss why you may have observed any similarities or differences (e.g. shared habitats, common plants, time of day of visit).

title: Field guide - final draft
text:
Overview
This is the final draft of your field guide. Use this as a checklist for the minimum components you should have in your field guide after the work you have done in previous assignments and incorporating the peer feedback you receive(d) in section.

title: Field guide - final draft
text:
Basic components
Your field guide must be hand made and written. Take this into account when you are designing the layout. Note that you have complete creative license in design! Consider a zine format, scrapbook, journal, etc. outside the bounds of regular blank paper.
At the beginning of your field guide, you should have:

a title page: the title, your name, and the year
a map of the region your field guide covers (i.e. the boundaries of the field site)
a list of species covered in the field guide
a final version of the interaction diagram you drew with two additional species (part 3 of the interaction diagram assignment)
a 3-5 sentence description of the interactions depicted in your diagram and their ecological basis

Each species in your field guide should have a separate entry. For each species entry, you should have:

visuals: drawings, paintings, collage, photographs etc. emphasizing important field marks for identification with arrows, boxes, highlighting, etc. Note: you must create your own visuals!
species description: measurements, components of anatomy, behavior, calls/songs (if applicable), etc. in your own words
habitat description: where the species might be found at the study site (1-2 sentences)
ecological description: what ecological role does this species occupy at the study site and/or in the region? (2-3 sentences)
in-text citations

Lastly, you should be sure to include:

a Works Cited or Reference page listing all the citations you used for your field guide



edited 2026-10-11: added requirement for citations






Citation format



You are free to use any citation format. You do not need to provide URLs for webpages; however, you should provide enough information such that someone could find the same page via a google search.

title: Field guide - final draft
text:
Presentation
The presentation of information in your field guide will be evaluated on:

cohesion: all pages have a cohesive look
narrative: your writing depicts the species and site accurately and with evidence to support your claims (i.e. with citations from field guides, articles, or other contextualizing texts appropriate for the assignment)
written communication: your writing is clear, free of grammatical errors

title: Field guide - final draft
text:
Creativity
You are welcome to be creative in the way you choose to present information in your field guide! This component is subjective, but reflective of your process in creating a final version of your field guide from the preparation assignments that preceded it. Creativity will be evaluated on the novelty with which you have presented your work and the execution of your original vision. You will make a case for both these points in your self-evaluation.

Project overview
This is the first of four project prep assignments for the field guide assignment. Your final field guide will be a guide to the 5 most common species in a given taxonomic group at the site of your choosing.

title: Site and species selection
text:
Assignment

1. Familiarize yourself with the sites we will visit in this class.
You can find a list of sites on the syllabus and on the site selection spreadsheet.


2. Sign up for two site × taxonomic group combinations.
For this and following steps, you will explore your options for two site × taxonomic group combinations. Your selections are not set in stone; however, you should give yourself the flexibility to explore two groups to ultimately choose one later on.


3. Articulate your reasoning for your choices.
In 1-3 sentences, describe:

why you are interested in these sites, with specific references to your own interests in ecosystems, experience, etc.
why you are interested in these taxonomic groups, again with specific references to your own interests
why you want to explore the taxonomic groups you chose at the sites you chose
how you personally might be able to transport yourself to these sites, if you needed to visit them (e.g. via bus, car, etc.) - be realistic about this!



4. Find the 5 most common species in each group at your chosen site(s).
Using iNaturalist, eBird, or any other observation database, find the most common species in your taxonomic group of choice at your sites.
For each site × taxonomic group combination, you should:

make a list of the 5 most common species
describe in 1-3 sentences how you found those species (for example, what filters or processes on iNaturalist did you use)

title: Methods of promoting observations
text:
Source credit



Much of the inspiration for note-taking and observation comes from common note-taking methods in ecological disciplines and John Muir Laws’s The Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling. If you’re interested in borrowing this text, let me know!
The information on this page comes from two sources by John Muir Laws: The Guide to Nature Drawing and Journaling and Opening the World Through Nature Journaling.
If you’re interested in developing your journaling practice further, I would highly recommend John Muir Laws’s work! He has many free videos walking through observation techniques, drawing, composition, etc.

title: Methods of promoting observations
text:
Promoting observation

I notice…
Examine whatever you are looking at. Start to say observations out loud. Do not filter anything out: if you see it, say it. Look at structure, behavior, color, interactions. Change your perspective: look up close or far away and see what else you can observe. If you find yourself running out of observations, challenge yourself to discover something new, or just say “I notice. . .” until an idea pops out. Pay attention to what surprises you. This gives you insight into ways that the world is different than you had thought.


I wonder…
After observing your object, start to come up with questions about it and say those out loud, too. Your questions might be connected to an observation you made earlier, or they could be about any aspect of what you’re observing. There is no need to worry about answering the questions yet. Just get them all out there. It’s okay if you continue to make-and say-observations as you come up with questions.


It reminds me of…
Last, say out loud everything that your object reminds you of. Allow yourself to be uninhibited in this step. Say anything that comes to mind: the object may have jarred your memory, reminding you of an experience you’ve had or a piece of information you already know, or the way it looks physically might remind you of something. Try looking at individual parts of the object, then back up and examine it as a whole.

title: Methods of promoting observations
text:
Interrogatives

Who: identity and identification
“Who made this nest?” “What kind of bird is that?”


What: describing events, trends, phenomena, behaviors
“What foraging strategies is this bird using?” “What is happening here?” “What happens when the sun comes out?”


Where: location (local and large scale)
“Do I spot this species at the forest edge or deep in the woods?” “Is this bird a resident or is it migrating?” “Where is it going next?” “Where will it spend the night?” “Is this nest hole oriented for protection from the wind or water?”
When: timing and phenology “What part of the nesting cycle are we in?” “How does the approaching winter play into what the bird is doing right now?” “How long can this cormorant hold its breath?” “How long does it take for the newt to crawl over a log?” “When did the flower turn into the fruit?”


How: mechanism or process
“How do those pelicans fly so close to the water without hitting the surface?” “How do bustits weave such delicate nests?”


Why: reason or meaning
“Why are the wings tilted up?” “Why are the leaves glossy?” “Why are these two individuals growing in such different locations?”
“Why” questions can be asked of any observation and are a good follow-up to other questions, to push inquiry deeper.
